item.title: Looking back over the whole track: better after turns, still worse on straight legs
item.description: Every tracker we tested since phase 3 worked in real time: it had to decide what the target was
item.content:encoded:
Every tracker we tested since phase 3 worked in real time: it had to decide what the target was doing using only the bearings so far. An analyst reconstructing an engagement afterwards can use all of them, including the bearings after each turn. So we trained a network that sees the whole window, and judged it against the classical tools for the same job: smoothers, and the best forward trackers.

What we found​

  • After turns, it is the best estimator we have. Its overall range and course errors are the lowest of anything tried. Course error falls by a third against our real-time network, because it no longer has to guess whether a turn has happened.
  • On straight legs, it is still well behind. Where the target holds course, its course error is 9°, against 3° for a well-tuned Kalman filter and 2° for batch least squares. The pre-registered rule asks it to match or come within 10% of every classical candidate on every check, so it stopped at validation.
  • The classical smoothers were not the obstacle. Tuned for range, they came out weaker than the forward filters. The forward filter alone settled the outcome.

What it means​

Looking back over the whole track does not change the project's answer. The network's strength is range, and course after a manoeuvre; classical methods remain better wherever the target holds course. The useful design is still the combination: a learned aid inside a classical method.

Results: experiments/20261120-p19-val/validation.md.

item.title: Teaching the detector to fire early: faster, but blind
item.description: Our trained manoeuvre detector had been taught that the whole five minutes after a turn count as
item.content:encoded:
Our trained manoeuvre detector had been taught that the whole five minutes after a turn count as "manoeuvring", which rewards a late, lingering alarm. So we retrained it to fire only in the first two minutes of a turn, and judged it exactly as before.

What we found​

  • It became fast. When it fires, it does so about 70 seconds into a turn: half the delay of the classical CUSUM detector on the turns both catch.
  • It became blind. Allowing one false alarm every two hours, it caught only 5% of turns within five minutes, against 12% for the CUSUM and 11% for the earlier version.
  • The two labels bracket the classical detector. One is about as complete but slower, the other faster but far less complete. Neither beats it.

What it means​

Under realistic bearing error, the turns that can be detected at all at a strict false-alarm rate are the ones a well-tuned classical detector already finds. The limit is the error, not how the network was taught. Manoeuvre detection stays the weak point of every design that relied on it.

Results: experiments/20261119-p18-val/validation.md.

item.title: A trained manoeuvre detector: no better than the classical one
item.description: Three of our designs stumbled on the same question: has the target just turned, or is the bearing
item.content:encoded:
Three of our designs stumbled on the same question: has the target just turned, or is the bearing error playing tricks? So we trained a network for exactly that question, on data with the realistic bearing error, and compared it with the best classical change detector (a CUSUM on a tracker's innovations) tuned to the same error.

What we found​

  • Every detector is weak when false alarms must be rare. Allowing one false alarm every two hours on quiet stretches, the best CUSUM spots only 12% of turns within 5 minutes. Under clean, uncorrelated error the figure was 28%.
  • The trained network did not beat it: 11% within 5 minutes, and slower on the turns both caught. It was no better than simply watching the tracking network's own course estimate (11%).
  • With more false alarms allowed the learned signals edge ahead. At two false alarms an hour they catch about 35% against the CUSUM's 33%. That is not the operating point we committed to.

What it means​

Correlated bearing error makes quiet legs look like gentle turns, and that, not the choice of detector, is the limit. This is why the composite solver and adaptive process noise failed, and a trained detector does not remove it. Training choices (rewarding early alarms rather than sustained ones, for instance) could still help, but nothing here suggests a large gain.

Results: experiments/20261118-p17-val/validation.md.

item.title: Fading the network on straight legs: the trade-off holds
item.description: The EKF fed with the network's range passed its gate overall, but on a target's straight leg it
item.content:encoded:
The EKF fed with the network's range passed its gate overall, but on a target's straight leg it was worse than the plain EKF. We tried two fixes together: let the network's weight fade once the bearings fix range, and let the filter's process noise rise only when the bearings look surprising (after a manoeuvre). A setting had to stay ahead overall and come within 10% of the EKF on straight legs. None did, so the phase stopped before using a fresh test set.

What we found​

  • Adapting the process noise just moves the trade-off. If it reacts readily, overall course recovers but straight-leg course gets worse; if it reacts rarely, the reverse. Under correlated bearing error, "surprising bearings" do not reliably mean a manoeuvre.
  • The fade does what it says, at a price. It brings straight-leg course from 4.0° to 3.6° (the EKF manages 3.1°) but gives up the network's range overall: 13.9% error instead of 12.5%.
  • Even with the reference's own process noise, adding the network costs about 20% on straight-leg course. Its range errors are correlated in time and leak into the velocity estimate.

What it means​

Straight legs belong to the classical methods (the EKF, and least squares even more so); the network's range helps after manoeuvres and overall. The phase-15 tracker stays the best compromise found. Splitting the work explicitly, a classical solution on straight legs and the fused tracker after manoeuvres, is what the composite solver tried earlier; its weak point was detecting the manoeuvre, the same weakness seen here.

Results: experiments/20261118-p16-val/validation.md.

item.title: The network's range inside an EKF beats the range-tuned EKF (with caveats)
item.description: Re-tuning the classical trackers to realistic bearing error stopped the IMM-based fused tracker:
item.content:encoded:
Re-tuning the classical trackers to realistic bearing error stopped the IMM-based fused tracker: after a target manoeuvre it held course worse than a plain EKF. So we fed the network's range estimate into an EKF instead, tuned its process noise together with the fusion weights on validation data, and judged the one chosen setting once on 40,000 fresh scenarios.

What we found​

  • It passed G5 against the re-tuned EKF. Range error 12.8% against 16.3% (0.78 ×) and course error 28.9° against 35.3° (0.82 ×) over all gate rows; on settled rows (pooled before and after manoeuvres), significantly worse on course than the EKF (1.04 ×, interval 1.01–1.08) but within the allowed 10% margin. We had forecast only a 10% chance of a pass.
  • The network is needed, but it is not the whole story. The same EKF with the higher process noise and no network fails the gate (a check run after scoring, reported only). About half the course gain comes from that process noise alone, which the reference, tuned for range, never used.
  • Straight legs still belong to the classical methods. Before any manoeuvre the plain EKF holds course to 3.3° and least squares to 2.2°; the fused tracker manages 5.2°. It wins after a manoeuvre (22° against 33°). The gate pools both, and the mix decides it.
  • It does not beat everything. Against the re-tuned IMM, course is level (0.99 ×). The network alone still has the lowest overall range (12.0%) and course (26.0°).

What it means​

The project's qualified go gets firmer: a learned range aid inside a classical tracker beats the EKF re-tuned (for range) to the same error, on range and overall course, though not the re-tuned IMM on course. It remains a range aid. On a long straight leg the network's correlated range error makes the tracker worse than bearings alone, so a weight that fades once the bearings fix range is the obvious next step.

Results: experiments/20261116-p15-g5/ and its panel review.

item.title: Re-arming the composite solver makes it worse
item.description: The first composite solver almost passed: it missed its gate by 1.3% on course. Its weakness
item.content:encoded:
The first composite solver almost passed: it missed its gate by 1.3% on course. Its weakness seemed clear. Once it handed over to the fused tracker after a manoeuvre, it never came back to least squares, even when the target settled on a new straight leg.

The owner chose to let it re-arm:

  • after a switch, fit a new straight leg, borrowing the fused tracker's range to pin it down;
  • hand back to that leg once it is a few minutes long and fits the bearings well.

Result: worse, not better​

  • The score. The best re-armed setting scores −0.031, against −0.013 for the original. It fails overall course against the fused tracker (1.034).
  • The pattern. Every setting does worse than without re-arming, and handing back sooner does worst.

Why​

  • The new legs look right but aren't. Where the composite uses one, it is about twice as wrong as the fused tracker on the same rows: range 31% against 16%, speed 5.9 kt against 3.0 kt.
  • A good fit isn't a right answer. Without the listening platform manoeuvring again, many different tracks explain a short leg's bearings equally well. Borrowing the range fixes the distance but not the velocity. This is the basic limit of bearings-only tracking, and it is why least squares needs an ownship manoeuvre in the first place.
  • The real cost is unchanged. 44% of the rows after a manoeuvre still come from the stale least-squares answer before the switch trips. Re-arming does nothing for those.

What it means​

Both composite designs are recorded as failing their gate on validation. No test data were generated. The lesson is narrow: a residual check can say when a straight-line fit has broken, but not when a new one is trustworthy.

Record: experiments/20261115-p12b-val/; SRD Annex D §D.7–D.8; spec 025.

item.title: A composite solver: the best of both, nearly — stopped at validation
item.description: Spec 024 found that batch least squares reaches the information limit while the target sails
item.content:encoded:
Spec 024 found that batch least squares reaches the information limit while the target sails straight, and that the fused tracker is best once the target has manoeuvred. The obvious next step was a composite:

  • report least squares while its straight-line fit still explains the bearings;
  • hand over to the fused tracker once the fit breaks.

The test​

  • The switch: a residual check over the last W bearings against a threshold c. Once tripped, it latches. Nothing is trained.
  • The gate (G9): better than the fused tracker overall on range and course, and within 1.1 × of least squares on straight legs, under realistic bearing error.
  • Pre-registration. W and c are picked on validation by a rule written down first. The composite goes to a fresh test set only if every check clears on validation.

Result: no setting clears all five checks​

The best setting (a 1-minute window, threshold 8) misses by 1.3% on overall course:

Composite againstRangeCourseSpeed
The fused tracker, all rows0.9641.0130.85 (reported)
Least squares, straight legs (limit 1.1)1.021.071.04

Why​

  • On straight legs it works. It keeps least squares' accuracy, with course errors 4 × smaller than the fused tracker's.
  • After a manoeuvre it pays for being late. Until the residual check trips, it keeps reporting least squares' out-of-date straight-line answer. Course there is 12% worse than the fused tracker's.
  • Most of the rows that count come after a manoeuvre, so the late switch outweighs the straight-leg gain on course.
  • Tuning the threshold only trades one failure for the other.
    • Switch earlier, and false alarms from the correlated error throw away least squares on straight legs.
    • Switch later, and the stale answers last longer.

This matches phase 5: detecting a manoeuvre from bearings alone is slow, whatever the detector.

What it means​

The composite is better than the fused tracker on range (about 4%) and clearly better on speed (about 15%). It is not better on course, and the pre-registered rule asked for all three. No test data were generated, and earlier results stand.

Possible next steps, each needing a new decision:

  • a gate that judges straight legs and post-manoeuvre rows separately;
  • a switch that can return to least squares on a new straight leg.

Record: experiments/20261115-p12-val/ (grid, diagnostic, slices); SRD Annex D; spec 025.

item.title: The project in plain English: can AI track a ship from bearings alone?
item.description: A non-technical summary of what this project set out to do, what it found, and what it means. The
item.content:encoded:
A non-technical summary of what this project set out to do, what it found, and what it means. The full, technical answer is the go/no-go report.

The question​

A submarine listening to a ship hears only which direction the sound comes from, not how far away the ship is. Working out the ship's range, course and speed from those directions alone is a classic problem called target motion analysis. Well-established mathematical methods already exist for it.

We asked whether an AI model, trained on large amounts of computer-simulated data, could do the job well enough to be useful.

How we worked​

Every step was set up as a fair test:

  • the rules were written down before the test ran;
  • the score came from fresh data the model had never seen;
  • the AI was always compared with the existing mathematical methods.

Each result was then checked by a panel of AI reviewers.

What we found​

  • The AI does learn something real. It clearly beats guesswork, and it is good at judging how far away the ship is.
  • On its own, it isn't good enough. When the ship sails straight, the traditional methods are 1.6 to 3.5 times more accurate, especially on speed. The AI never caught up, despite many attempts.
  • It shines where the traditional methods struggle. That is in the minutes just after the ship turns, and when the direction measurements carry realistic, drifting errors.
  • The best result combines the two. Feeding the AI's range estimate into a traditional tracker made it 18–23% more accurate on range than the tracker alone.
  • A final check measured the theoretical best possible accuracy.
    • On straight legs, the traditional method already reaches that limit, and the AI is about 1.5 times worse.
    • After the ship turns, it is still unknown how much better anything could do.

The verdict​

  • No: the AI should not replace the traditional methods.
  • A qualified yes: it is worth using as a helper inside a traditional tracker, mainly for judging range and for coping after the ship turns.

What would come next​

The next step is testing on real or more realistic data, against a traditional tracker tuned for those conditions. That cannot happen here, because this project is public and uses simulated data only.

Honest caveats​

  • Everything is simulated.
  • Some rules were relaxed along the way. That always happened before the affected result was known, but it still matters.
  • The reviewers were not fully independent. They were AI agents of the same family as the one doing the work.

None of these changes the main "no".

item.title: Re-tuning the classical trackers: the fused tracker's course falls short
item.description: The severity sweep showed that the classical trackers we compared against had been tuned on white
item.content:encoded:
The severity sweep showed that the classical trackers we compared against had been tuned on white noise, which flattered the fused tracker. So we re-tuned both of them, the IMM and the EKF, to the realistic bearing error, then rebuilt the fused tracker on the re-tuned IMM and tried its 24 fusion settings again. To go to a gate, a setting had to beat both re-tuned trackers on G5's five checks.

What we found​

  • Re-tuning helps the classical trackers a little. Range error falls from 16.1% to 15.8% for the EKF and from 16.7% to 15.1% for the IMM. Both do it by treating the correlated error as heavier white noise.
  • The fused tracker's range advantage survives. Its best setting has 12.5% range error: 0.79 × the EKF's and 0.83 × the IMM's.
  • Its course after a manoeuvre does not. Once the target has settled, the re-tuned EKF holds course to 8.3°; the best fused tracker manages 10.7°, 1.29 × the EKF and over the 1.1 limit. No setting comes close enough, so the phase stopped before the gate, as forecast.
  • Against the re-tuned IMM alone it would have passed validation. Choosing the harder of the two references decided the outcome.

What it means​

The network improves range; the IMM it feeds still sets the course, and a plain EKF does that better on settled legs. The fused tracker is a range aid, not a better tracker overall. One condition of the project's qualified go, a fair re-tuned reference, is not met; the owner decides what follows. Fusing the network's range into the EKF instead is the obvious untried design.

Results: experiments/20261115-p14-val/validation.md.

item.title: How the trackers cope as bearing error gets worse
item.description: The project's "qualified go" for the fused tracker rested on one level of realistic bearing
item.content:encoded:
The project's "qualified go" for the fused tracker rested on one level of realistic bearing error. We re-ran every frozen estimator on the same scenarios at four levels: no correlated error (×0), half (×0.5), the usual level (×1) and double (×2).

What we found​

  • The fused tracker keeps its edge over the classical IMM at every level: its range error is 0.84, 0.79, 0.78 and 0.77 × the IMM's. The edge grows a little, then levels off.
  • Batch least squares stays at the information limit on straight legs at every level. Nothing can do better there.
  • The network on its own overtakes the fused tracker as error grows. At ×0 the fused tracker is better; at ×0.5 they tie; at ×2 the network alone has 20% less range error. The fused tracker inherits the IMM's weakness under heavy error, and its settings were chosen on white noise.
  • The composite solver's switch breaks under heavy error. Correlated error looks like a manoeuvre to its fit check, so at ×2 it gives up least squares on straight legs.

What it means​

The qualified go survives. Two conditions get sharper: the fusion's settings, and the classical reference it is judged against, both need tuning to the error level of real data. Part of the network's robustness is a learned prior about typical geometry, which only helps while real engagements look like the simulated ones.

Results: experiments/20261115-p13-sweep/results.md.

item.title: Phase 11: retraining T2 on realistic bearing error does not improve its range
item.description: Phases 7–10 showed that under realistic bearing error (correlated noise plus a drifting bias), the
item.content:encoded:
Phases 7–10 showed that under realistic bearing error (correlated noise plus a drifting bias), the learned network T2 gives the most robust range estimate. T2 had been trained only on white noise. The obvious next question: does training it on the realistic error make it better still?

The test​

  • The model. T2's architecture and configuration, unchanged, trained from scratch on a fresh 100,000-scenario dataset generated entirely with realistic error. Training took about 16 hours on GitHub Actions and stopped early at epoch 48.
  • The gate (G8). The retrained T2 must:
    • have a median range error wholly below the frozen T2's;
    • pass G5 against the reference IMM.
  • The validation step first. The six point estimates on the shared validation split must all be within their limits before any test data are generated.

Result: no gain on range, so it stops at validation​

Retrained T2 againstRangeCourseSettled course
The frozen T21.021 [0.991, 1.052]0.9810.878
The IMM0.7450.8571.079
  • Range is unchanged. 12.4% against the frozen T2's 12.2%, and the interval also rules out a gain of more than 1%.
  • Settled course improves by about 12%, mostly on straight legs before any manoeuvre.
  • It still beats the IMM on overall range and course, and passes G5's settled limits.

The cost: worse on white noise​

On the same scenarios with white noise only, the retrained T2 is clearly worse:

Median range errorWhite noiseRealistic error
Retrained T210.3%12.4%
Frozen T28.0%12.2%
IMM9.1%16.7%

The retrained T2 looks more robust (it degrades 1.21 × against 1.52 ×), but only because it starts worse. On white noise it loses to the IMM on range.

Baselines (realistic error, all gated rows)​

  • Batch least squares: 17.1% and 46.0°. It is best before any manoeuvre (6.9%, 2.0°).
  • EKF: 16.1% and 29.7°. It is best on settled course (9.8°) and speed (1.91 kt).
  • Naive: 38.7% and 88.3°.
  • Fused tracker and hybrid: rebuilt on the retrained T2, they are unchanged (within 0.3 points in range).

What it means​

Seeing the error in training did not buy range accuracy. A plausible reading is that the frozen T2 is already near what the bearings allow under this error model: phase 9 found the drifting bias nearly unobservable, and a network cannot learn what the data do not contain.

Limits:

  • one training run, so the run-to-run spread is unknown;
  • one error model at one severity;
  • validation data only;
  • an architecture that was not re-tuned.

No test data were generated. Phase 10's verdict stands, and the owner decides what comes next.

Record: experiments/20261114-p11-val/ (diagnostic, baselines, clean twin); model experiments/20261113-p11a-models/; decision experiments/20261113-p11-decision/; spec 023; SRD Annex C §C.18.

item.title: Phase 10: T2's range with a filter's velocity passes G8, but adds little that was not known
item.description: Phases 7–9 left one clear lesson. Under realistic bearing error (correlated noise plus a drifting
item.content:encoded:
Phases 7–9 left one clear lesson. Under realistic bearing error (correlated noise plus a drifting bias), the learned network T2 gives the most robust range, and no change to the filters closes the gap. Phase 10 takes the direct route and reports T2's range alongside the fused tracker's course and speed.

The test​

  • The estimator:

    • range and position from T2;
    • course and speed from the frozen fused tracker;
    • T2's whole row wherever the fused tracker has no estimate (0.9% of the gated rows, 2.5% of all rows).

    Nothing is trained or tuned.

  • The gate (G8): pass G5 against the reference IMM, and have a median range error wholly below the fused tracker's.

  • Pre-registration. The rules, the validation run and the decision record were all committed before the test data existed.

Result: G8 passes (seed 224, 40,000 scenarios)​

Hybrid againstRangeCourseSettled rangeSettled courseSettled speed
The IMM (limit 1 / 1.1)0.6890.8950.7240.8870.898
The fused tracker (limit 1)0.908 [0.893, 0.921]

The checks use 67,292 rows from the 20,161 test scenarios at σ = 1°. T2 converged on every row. Every 97.5% interval sits wholly within its limit. Five independent reviewers agreed that the verdict is right.

Why this is mostly a replay​

The panel was blunt about how much this pass adds:

  • The range is T2's, row for row. The check against the fused tracker is therefore T2 against the fused tracker. Phase 7 already showed that (fused/T2 1.095), and phase 8 showed no tuning closes it. Seed 224 replicates that result.
  • The velocity is the fused tracker's, which already passed G5 in phase 7.
  • The estimator to beat changed. In phases 8–9 it was T2; here it is the fused tracker, by the owner's choice before validation. T2 is still not beaten on range.
  • What is new is only that the pair, assembled per output, passes every G5 check at once.
  • About 1 point of each margin comes from the scoring convention. A row with no estimate counts as infinitely wrong, and the hybrid never lacks one. On rows where every estimator converged the ratios are 0.700 against the IMM and 0.918 against the fused tracker. Both still pass.

What it does not show​

Median error, all G5 rowsRangeCourseSpeed
Hybrid12.0%26.6°2.58 kt
Fused tracker13.2%27.1°2.60 kt
T2 alone12.0%25.9°2.85 kt
IMM17.4%29.7°2.87 kt
EKF16.6%30.2°2.41 kt
Batch least squares18.0%46.6°2.50 kt
Naive40.2%89.9°3.99 kt
  • No gain over T2 on range, since the range is T2's. T2 alone is also slightly better on overall course.
  • Classical filters still win on straight legs. The EKF is better on settled course (10.7° against 13.3°) and speed. Before any manoeuvre, batch least squares is best (7.3%, 2.2°).
  • It is not a track. The position comes from one estimator and the velocity from another. The position change over a minute disagrees with the stated velocity by a median 18 kt (8 kt for the fused tracker; 17 kt for T2 alone, whose position track is itself jumpy), and the implied bearing rate is the worst of the four estimators. It is a set of per-output estimates, not a state you could extrapolate.
  • No uncertainty is stated for the combined estimate.
  • Scope: one error model at one severity, on simulated data.

The arc, phases 7–10​

Under realistic bearing error:

  • the learned range estimate is the most robust;
  • feeding it into a filter costs some of that robustness;
  • tuning the fusion doesn't recover it;
  • modelling the bias inside the filter fails, because the bias can't be observed.

Reporting the learned range directly keeps its accuracy, at the cost of a coherent track.

Record: experiments/20261112-p10-g8/ (verdict, baselines, coherence, panel review); validation experiments/20261112-p10-val/; decision experiments/20261112-p10-decision/; spec 022.

item.title: Phase 9: a bias-aware IMM cannot see the bias
item.description: Under realistic bearing error (correlated noise plus a drifting bias), the learned range estimate
item.content:encoded:
Under realistic bearing error (correlated noise plus a drifting bias), the learned range estimate T2 beat the classical IMM, and no fusion setting could close the gap (phase 8). The natural classical answer is to model the error: give the IMM a sixth state for the bearing bias and let it estimate the bias.

The test​

  • The filter: the reference IMM, plus a drifting bias added to every predicted bearing.
  • Tuning: the bias's size and time constant and the measurement noise scale, 18 settings in all, on validation data with realistic error.
  • The rule, fixed before any setting was scored: to go to a gate, a setting must beat T2 on range and still pass G5 against the plain IMM.
  • The forecast, recorded beforehand: this would probably fail. A quick check had shown that a 1° offset barely changes how well a straight-line track fits the bearings.

Result: it stops at validation​

Bias-state IMMvs plain IMM, rangevs T2, range
Best setting (0.25°, 10 min, r 8)0.9981.37
Larger bias (1°)1.05–1.121.44–1.53
  • At best it matches the plain IMM. It never improves on it.
  • It stays about 1.4 × T2's range error.
  • Allowing a larger bias makes it worse. The extra freedom is not pinned down by the bearings.

Why​

From bearings alone, a slowly drifting bias looks almost exactly like a slightly rotated target track. One or two ownship zigs do not separate the two, so the filter cannot learn the bias. T2 does better on range, plausibly because it learns range from the whole bearing history. That explanation was not tested.

Where this leaves things​

Phases 7–9 tell one story. Under this error model:

  • the learned range is the most robust estimate;
  • fusing it into a filter that assumes white noise loses some of that advantage;
  • modelling the bias inside the filter does not help, because the bias cannot be observed.

Two options remain for the owner:

  • report T2's range directly, as a hybrid;
  • close out the project.

Record: experiments/20261112-p9-research/; spec 021; SRD Annex C §C.16.

item.title: Phase 8: re-tuning the fusion cannot make it beat T2 on range under realistic error
item.description: Phase 7 found a gap. Under realistic bearing error (correlated noise plus a drifting bias), T2 on
item.content:encoded:
Phase 7 found a gap. Under realistic bearing error (correlated noise plus a drifting bias), T2 on its own had lower range error than the fused tracker that feeds T2's range into the IMM: 12.1% against 13.2%. The fusion's weighting had been tuned on clean data and then frozen, so the obvious question was whether re-tuning it closes the gap.

The test​

The owner chose to re-tune only the fusion's two settings, on validation data with realistic error:

  • k, how much to trust T2's range;
  • M, how often to feed it in.

The gate would require both of these:

  • beat T2 alone on median range error;
  • still pass G5 against the reference IMM.

The grid had 24 settings. The rule for choosing between them was written and committed before any of them was scored. A setting went to the gate only if its estimated margin on every check was positive.

Result: no setting qualifies​

SettingFused / IMM rangeFused / T2 range
Frozen (k 4, every 6 samples)0.7771.064
Best re-tune (k 3, every sample)0.7401.014
Heaviest weight on T2 (k 0.5, every sample)0.7491.027
  • Re-tuning helps against the IMM. Feeding T2's range at every sample cuts the fused tracker's range error further (0.74 × the IMM's), and cuts its shortfall against T2 from 6.4% to 1.4%.
  • It never beats T2. The best setting is still 1.4% worse on range. Trusting T2 more does not help either: course and velocity then fall apart (course up to 1.27 × the IMM's on settled rows), and range still trails T2.
  • So phase 8 stops at validation. No fresh test data were generated, and phase 7's verdict stands.

Why, plausibly​

Under the drifting bias, the IMM's range ends up about 7% short. Every bearing update pulls the shared track state back towards that biased range, so a single filter state cannot hold T2's less biased range, however the two are weighted. This explanation was not tested here.

What it means​

Within this design, fusing T2's range into a filter that assumes white noise costs some range accuracy under correlated error. The filter's state stays coherent, and it still beats the IMM clearly.

Two further changes might close the gap:

  • a filter that models the bias;
  • reporting T2's range directly, as the phase-4b hybrid did.

Either would be a new decision for the owner.

Record: experiments/20261110-p8-research/ (grid, selection, validation note); spec 020; SRD Annex C §C.15.

item.title: Phase 7: realistic bearing error — the frozen fused tracker still beats the frozen IMM, but T2 alone is more robust
item.description: So far every tracker in this project has seen only white bearing noise. Real bearings also carry
item.content:encoded:
So far every tracker in this project has seen only white bearing noise. Real bearings also carry correlated error and a slowly drifting bias. Phase 7 asks one question: does the fused tracker's G5 advantage over the reference IMM survive that error, with nothing re-trained or re-tuned?

The setup​

The owner chose three things:

  • frozen trackers;
  • an error model made of a correlated term (sd 1.0°, 30 s) and a drifting bias (sd 0.5°, 20 min). This setting is double the one first proposed. At σ = 1° the total bearing error goes from 1.0° to 1.5°;
  • G5's rules, unchanged.

The generator adds the error from its own random stream, so each scenario can be regenerated without it. The two versions have identical geometry and identical white noise, which makes a paired clean comparison possible.

Result: G5 passes (seed 218, 40,000 scenarios)​

Fused / IMMRatio (97.5% CI)Limit
Overall range0.766 [0.755, 0.778]< 1
Overall course0.907 [0.897, 0.918]< 1
Settled range0.774< 1.1
Settled course0.875< 1.1
Settled speed0.907< 1.1

Validation on seed 217 had already shown much the same: 0.777 for range and 0.922 for course. Five independent reviewers agreed the verdict is right, and one reproduced it byte for byte.

What the pass does not show​

The absolute errors are large: the fused tracker's 90th-percentile course error is 106°. The panel narrowed the claim.

Median error, all G5 rowsRangeCourseSpeed
Fused tracker13.2%27°2.6 kt
IMM (reference)17.3%30°2.9 kt
T2 alone12.1%26°2.9 kt
EKF16.8%31°2.4 kt
Batch least squares17.6%47°2.4 kt
Naive40%90°3.9 kt
  • T2 alone beats the fused tracker on range, by 1.10 × [1.08, 1.11] overall. Its error grows least under realistic error (1.47 × its clean value, against the IMM's 1.82 ×). The IMM's range ends up biased about 7% short under the drifting bias, while T2 stays nearly unbiased. The fusion setting, frozen from clean data, plausibly gives T2 too little weight; k was not re-swept. Fusing keeps one coherent track state, but under this error it is not the best range estimator.
  • On straight legs, classical methods still win. On settled rows the EKF beats the fused tracker on course (10.6° against 13.5°) and on speed, and batch least squares does too (8.1°, 1.8 kt). Before any manoeuvre, batch least squares is best of all: 7.3% range and 2.2° course.
  • The reference was frozen, not adapted. Neither filter models correlated or bias error. An IMM with an inflated measurement noise or a bias state might close the gap; this phase does not test that.
  • Every tracker is much worse. Median range error rises 1.5–1.8 × overall and about 2 × on settled rows.
  • Not measured. Filter consistency (NIS, NEES) and covariance health (non-PD steps) under correlated error.
  • Scope. The result covers one error model at one severity, σ = 1° rows and simulated data.

The one-line version​

Under one setting of realistic bearing error, the frozen fused tracker keeps its G5 advantage over the frozen IMM, which was not adapted to this error. The learned range (T2) is likely what makes it robust (a hypothesis), and on its own T2 is more robust still. The classical filters remain better on straight legs.

Record: experiments/20261108-p7-g5/ (verdict, baselines, clean comparison, panel review); validation experiments/20261108-p7-val/; decision experiments/20261108-p7-decision/; G0 experiments/20261108-g0-p7-r1/; spec 019.

item.title: Phase 6 re-score: G7 passes, with coverage within tolerance on average but not calibrated
item.description: G7 on seed 215 was inconclusive: the fused tracker's 50% range interval covered 48.3%, and its
item.content:encoded:
G7 on seed 215 was inconclusive: the fused tracker's 50% range interval covered 48.3%, and its confidence interval straddled the 48% floor. The rules allow one re-score on a larger fresh seed. The owner chose to run it. Decision 34 fixed the details before the data existed:

  • What stayed the same: the tracker, the reference, the frozen models, the multipliers and the rules.
  • What changed: a fresh seed, 216, and a test split of 110,000 scenarios instead of 40,000. That is large enough to resolve a coverage of about 48.3% against the floor.
  • The forecast: about an even chance of passing.

Result: pass​

Coverage on seed 216 (184,667 G5 rows)50%90%
Range (log)48.6% [48.3, 48.9]89.9%
Course50.5%90.3%
Speed49.4%89.9%

All nine gated checks pass. The fused tracker's 90% intervals are narrower than the IMM's: 0.73 × for range, 0.94 × for course and 0.89 × for speed. This was the one re-score, so the verdict is final.

What the pass does and does not show​

Five independent reviewers agreed that the pass is correct. One recomputed every value with code of its own, and another re-ran the gate. All five also agreed on how far the claim goes.

  • Range intervals run about 1.5 points short. At 50%, the two seeds together give about 48.5% [48.3, 48.8]. That is inside the ±2-point tolerance but not centred on 50%. The pass rests on the tolerance. The reference IMM, fitted on the same validation data, lands on 50%. So reusing validation data does not explain the fused tracker's shortfall.

  • The intervals cover within tolerance only on the pooled mix of rows. Range at 50% covers:

    RowsCoverage
    Settled, before any manoeuvre (quiet legs)67%
    Settled, after a manoeuvre39%
    At zig + 5 min61%
    At zig + 20 min40%

    Seed 215 showed the same pattern within a point.

  • Course and speed intervals are often uninformative.

    • 17% of course 90% intervals span the whole circle, and the median course 90% interval is 188° wide. The course width ratio of 0.94 therefore compares two mostly vague intervals.
    • 27% of speed 90% intervals reach below zero.

  • This was a second look. Over both seeds, the chance of a false pass is about 5% at most, not 2.5%. A smaller re-score would probably have been inconclusive again.

  • The pass judges these frozen multipliers. The 0.3-point margin is smaller than the multipliers' own sampling error. So the pass does not show that the recalibration procedure works in general.

Phase 6 in one line​

On average over the G5 rows, the fused tracker's recalibrated intervals cover within the tolerance, with range about 1.5 points short, and they are tighter than the IMM's. Within a regime they do not: the intervals are too wide on quiet legs and too narrow after a manoeuvre, and its course intervals are often vacuous. Conditional calibration, for example a multiplier that depends on time since the last manoeuvre, would be a new design. The owner decides on the follow-on.

Record: experiments/20261106-p6v-g7/ (verdict, regimes, panel review); decision experiments/20261106-p6v-rescore-decision/; spec 018.

item.title: Phase 6: the fused tracker's uncertainty, recalibrated, is inconclusive at G7
item.description: C.6's second follow-on asks whether the tracker that passed G5 can say how sure it is. The fused
item.content:encoded:
C.6's second follow-on asks whether the tracker that passed G5 can say how sure it is. The fused tracker is the frozen IMM with T2's range fused in.

The owner chose two things:

  • Calibrate the fused tracker's stated uncertainty, without training.
  • The test: calibrated and sharper. Its 50% and 90% intervals for range, course and speed must cover within ±2 points of nominal, and be narrower than the reference IMM's after the same recalibration.

What was done​

  • Stated sds. Both trackers now write them, from their covariance by the delta method. They are badly miscalibrated as stated: typical errors are a fraction of the stated sd, with heavy tails.
  • Recalibration, post hoc. One pair of multipliers per output, fitted on validation, scales the sd into 50% and 90% intervals. A two-fold check on validation passed, and decision 33 froze the multipliers before seed 215 was generated for scoring.

Result: inconclusive​

Coverage on seed 215 (G5 rows)50%90%
Range (log)48.3% [47.8, 48.8]89.8%
Course50.5%90.2%
Speed49.3%89.6%

The fused tracker's intervals are narrower than the IMM's: 0.73 × for range, 0.95 × for course and 0.89 × for speed. Eight of the nine checks pass. Range at 50% falls just short: its interval straddles the 48% floor.

What the panel added​

Five independent reviewers agreed the verdict is right, and reproduced it byte for byte. They also narrowed what can be claimed:

  • The intervals are calibrated only on the pooled mix of rows. On quiet straight legs before any manoeuvre they are far too wide: range 50% covers 67%. After a manoeuvre they are too narrow: 38%. One multiplier cannot fix that shape.
  • Course and speed intervals are often uninformative. 17% of course 90% intervals span the whole circle, and 27% of speed 90% intervals reach below zero.
  • The shortfall looks systematic, not noise. The likely cause is that T2's training epoch, the fusion settings and the multipliers were all chosen on the same validation split.
  • The rules were the agent's. The owner did not get to review them before the decision record.

What next​

The rules allow one re-score on a larger fresh seed. It would probably land near 48.3% again, so a pass would mean the range coverage just reaches the floor, not that the tracker is well calibrated. The owner decides whether to run it.

Record: experiments/20261106-p6u-g7/; spec 018.

item.title: Phase 5: frozen models do not beat a CUSUM at detecting manoeuvres
item.description: G5 passed in phases 4b and 4c. SRD Annex C §C.6 therefore lists incremental follow-ons, and the
item.content:encoded:
G5 passed in phases 4b and 4c. SRD Annex C §C.6 therefore lists incremental follow-ons, and the first is manoeuvre detection, judged against a CUSUM on the reference tracker's innovations.

The owner chose two things for this attempt:

  • No training. The detector is built from models that already exist: the frozen recurrent tracker T2, and the reference IMM, which now uses decision 32's guarded initialisation.
  • The test. Detection delay, with every detector's threshold set for the same false-alarm rate: one alarm per 2 h of quiet tracking.

What was compared​

  • The baseline. A CUSUM on the IMM's innovations, tuned on validation from 12 declared settings to favour it.
    • Clipping. The innovations are heavy-tailed: a few huge values otherwise hold an alarm for hours. So both the variance kind and the mean-shift kind are clipped.
    • The winner. The two-sided mean-shift CUSUM, since a turn biases the bearings to one side.
  • The learned detectors. Two candidates, declared in advance:
    • T2's course disagreement with the IMM;
    • T2's own course change over the last minute.

Result: it stopped at validation​

At 0.5 false alarms per hour, on 7,479 course changes in seed-211 validation:

Detected within 5 min
CUSUM (mean shift)28.2%
T2's course change over 1 min19.2%
T2 against the IMM5.9%
  • The learned detector is not carried. It is 9 points behind, with interval [−10.2, −7.7] pp, so it was not taken to a test split, and fresh seed 215 was never generated.
  • The delay check could not be judged. Every detector misses more than half the course changes at this rate, so the median delays are infinite. That rule was the agent's, written before the data; any later attempt should declare a delay statistic defined at its operating point.

Reported, not used: a crossover​

The same detectors were also calibrated at looser rates:

False alarms per hour0.5125
CUSUM28.2%38.0%47.8%62.6%
T2's course change19.2%39.0%58.1%71.7%

From about 1 false alarm per hour, T2's course change catches more manoeuvres in time, though about 20–40 s later among those both catch. Moving the operating point after seeing this would choose the rule from the result, so it stays a reported observation.

What next​

The owner decides. Annex C's other follow-ons remain:

  • calibration of the learned uncertainty;
  • realistic bearing error.

Record: experiments/20261105-p5-research/validation.md; spec 017.

item.title: Phase 4c: one track, a tracker that listens to a network's range
item.description: Phase 4b's hybrid passed G5, but it was two estimators stitched together: T2's range beside the
item.content:encoded:
Phase 4b's hybrid passed G5, but it was two estimators stitched together: T2's range beside the IMM's velocity. Phase 4c keeps one filter. The frozen IMM takes the frozen network T2's range as an extra measurement, weighted by T2's own stated uncertainty and inflated four-fold, once a minute. Nothing was trained.

It passed G5 on a fresh 40,000-scenario test split (seed 214), decided by the agent review panel:

Fused tracker / IMM, 97.5% intervalLimitResult
Range, all gate rows< 10.82 [0.81, 0.84]
Course, all gate rows< 10.95 [0.94, 0.96]
Range, settled rows< 1.10.86 [0.84, 0.89]
Course, settled rows< 1.10.95 [0.93, 0.97]
Speed, settled rows< 1.10.90 [0.87, 0.92]

Records: the gate record and the panel review.

What improved on phase 4b​

  • One state. Range, course and speed come from one filter. Projected forward, its bearing stays as close to the truth as the IMM's own (1.02° after 5 min against 1.06°), where the hybrid's drifted to 1.49°.
  • Settled rows improved because of estimation, not copying. Settled range, course and speed are all better than the IMM's and the hybrid's. The hybrid's settled velocity was mostly the IMM's.
  • The hybrid's worst case is gone. Before any target manoeuvre the hybrid's range was 1.43 × the IMM's. The fused tracker's is 1.03 × [0.99, 1.07]: parity.

What it does not show​

  • It does not beat the IMM before a target manoeuvres. On validation it seemed to (0.94 ×), but on the fresh seed it only matches it. The gains come after manoeuvres: 0.74 × the IMM's range error there.
  • The EKF and batch least squares are still better before any manoeuvre. Against the EKF it would fail settled course (1.41 ×). Overall it beats the EKF by a wide margin (range 0.80 ×, course 0.78 ×).
  • The hybrid is still better on overall course (fused 1.04 × the hybrid).
  • The settings were chosen in-sample, from 18 variants on validation. The decision record says 12; the panel found the error after scoring, and it is corrected around the frozen record. Only the fresh seed decides, and it did.
  • Its uncertainty is not calibrated. Like the IMM's, its covariance is too wide on typical rows and too narrow in a small tail.
  • It is not a learned tracker. It is a filter that listens to a frozen network. Phases 4b and 4c use the same T2 and IMM, so they are not independent replications. Both show that T2's range helps this IMM. Neither shows that a network alone tracks better.

The long view​

After G0 to G5 and three phase-4 attempts:

  • What networks add. A learned range estimate is genuinely useful to a tuned tracker, mostly after the target manoeuvres. Folded into the filter as a measurement, it gives one consistent track that beats the tuned IMM on every G5 check.
  • What they do not do. On clean, straight-leg geometry the classical tools (an EKF, a batch fit) remain better.

Real or recorded data are still the untested step.

item.title: Phase 4: an end-to-end learned tracker wins overall, loses on straight legs
item.description: Phase 4 asked whether a learned tracker, trained end to end, could beat a tuned IMM tracker on
item.content:encoded:
Phase 4 asked whether a learned tracker, trained end to end, could beat a tuned IMM tracker on targets that manoeuvre up to three times. Two trackers were trained from scratch and compared with the frozen reference on the same validation split:

  • T1, a learned-gain filter: Kalman-style physics with a gain computed by a small recurrent network;
  • T2, a pure recurrent tracker (2 × 128 LSTM) that also states its own uncertainty.

Neither reached the test. The pre-registered rule needs every gated check to pass on validation.

Median error, ratio to the IMMLimitT2T1
Range, all gate rows< 10.852.18
Course, all gate rows< 10.841.32
Range, settled rows< 1.10.972.80
Course, settled rows< 1.11.442.12
Speed, settled rows< 1.11.662.30

"Settled" rows are at least five minutes after the target's last manoeuvre. Both of T2's failures have their whole 97.5% interval above the limit, so the fresh test split (seed 212) was never scored.

Record: the validation record.

What was tested​

  • Data. Generator 0.5.0 gives the target 0–3 course changes and, in 30% of scenarios, a speed change, in 20–60 min windows.
  • Reference. An IMM (constant velocity plus coordinated turn), tuned on validation over all gate rows and frozen. Its median range error there is 9.2%.
  • Gate rows. σ = 1° bearings at 5, 10, 15 and 20 min after ownship's zig.
  • Forecast, recorded before training: T1 carried with probability about 35%, T2 about 10%, G5 passed about 20%.

What happened​

T2 is the best estimator yet on manoeuvring targets.

  • Range. 7.8% median against the IMM's 9.2%. The lead grows with time and with each turn: at 20 min after the zig, 10.8% against 16.6%.
  • Course. After three turns, 34° against the IMM's 46°.
  • Gross errors. 3.5 percentage points fewer than the IMM.
  • Its stated uncertainty is honest. 71% of its errors fall within one stated standard deviation (68% expected) and 95% within two (95% expected).

On straight legs it still loses. On settled rows its speed error is 2.16 kt against the IMM's 1.30 kt, and its course error 10.7° against 7.4°. Before the first manoeuvre the gap is widest: 2.0 kt against 0.7 kt.

T1 never learned range. Its range error is 19–22% at every gate time and does not fall after ownship's zig, as a working tracker's does.

  • Why. Its gain is expressed along and across the line of sight. The cross term is kept positive, so the bearing loop is stable at any range. The range term has to change sign with the geometry, and the network did not learn that from what it saw.
  • The first run diverged in epoch 0. It was fixed before any result was seen, and the fix is recorded as an amendment to the decision.

Reading it critically​

  • This is the third time the same pattern has appeared. Phases 3, 3b and now 4 each found a network that beats a tuned tracker after manoeuvres and gives accuracy back when the target holds course. More turns per scenario moved the overall checks in the network's favour; they did not touch the straight-leg deficit.
  • The settled gap is mostly speed. A Kalman filter on a straight leg gets velocity almost for free from a long, consistent bearing history. The networks have the same history but do not match it, even with a speed loss weight of 4.
  • A stronger straight-leg reference exists. Batch least squares reaches 6.7% settled range, better than both the IMM and T2. The settled checks compare against a reference that is not the best achievable there.
  • The gate asked for dominance, not a trade. On a mix of manoeuvring and straight targets, T2 is better overall and worse when settled. Whether that trade is useful is an operational question that G5 deliberately did not answer.
  • Training was slower and less robust than planned. There were four restarts: a diverging filter, a 2 GiB file limit, a refused cross-commit resume and a lost CI runner. None changed a result. T2's fresh run reproduced its first run's epochs to the last digit.

What next​

SRD Annex C leaves the follow-on to the owner if G5 is not passed. Options include:

  • A hybrid. T2's manoeuvre advantage switched in only when it reports high uncertainty or a manoeuvre, with the tracker otherwise, as G3's hybrid did for classical estimates.
  • A narrower question. Manoeuvre detection and recovery only, where the network already wins.
  • Stopping here and writing up the programme.

Real or recorded data stay deferred.
